step1_summary: Chief complaint: Progressive hearing loss in left ear for ~6 weeks.

Symptoms: Unilateral (left) decreased hearing; intermittent left-sided tinnitus; occasional mild dizziness/lightheadedness with some nausea; symptoms on/off over 6 weeks; patient reports prior brief episode (~1 year ago) lasting a couple of days.

Onset/duration/severity/aggravating-alleviating: Gradual/insidious onset over six weeks, intermittent. Sound (watching TV/listening to music) can mask/relieve the tinnitus. Dizziness is mild (not true spinning), not associated with chest pain or palpitations.
Past medical history: Not reported / not documented in transcript.
Medications / Allergies: Not reported / not documented.
Family / Social history: Not reported / not documented.
Vital signs / Exam: None recorded in transcript; doctor plans in-person otoscopic ear exam.
Labs / Imaging: None performed or reported.

V: Vertebrobasilar insufficiency / brainstem ischemia: unilateral hearing changes and vestibular symptoms can result from posterior circulation ischemia—relevant to dizziness + hearing loss, though presentation here is subacute and intermittent.
I: Otitis media / externa or viral cochleitis/labyrinthitis: inflammation/infection of middle/inner ear can cause unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and dizziness; often accompanied by pain/fever/discharge (which are absent here) but mild/atypical presentations possible.

Cerumen impaction (obstructive cause listed here as common inflammatory/obstructive ear cause): can cause unilateral muffled hearing and tinnitus and is commonly suspected by examiner in the transcript.
N: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) / CPA tumor: typically causes unilateral progressive hearing loss, unilateral tinnitus, and balance symptoms—fits the unilateral tinnitus/hearing loss with mild imbalance.
D: Noise-induced or sensorineural hearing loss (idiopathic cochlear degeneration): could present with unilateral tinnitus and hearing change, less typical in younger patient but possible.
I2: Ototoxicity from drugs (aminoglycosides, high-dose loop diuretics, cisplatin, etc.): can cause tinnitus and hearing loss; relevant if there were exposures, but no medication use reported in transcript.
C: Congenital inner-ear malformation: less likely to present de novo in adulthood but can account for unilateral hearing deficits if previously subclinical.
A: Autoimmune inner ear disease: can cause progressive sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus; usually more rapidly progressive and often bilateral but unilateral presentations occur.
T: Barotrauma / prior head trauma: can cause unilateral hearing changes and vestibular symptoms if there was relevant history (none reported).
E: Metabolic/endocrine causes (e.g., thyroid disease, diabetes-related neuropathy): can contribute to hearing changes but less specific for unilateral tinnitus/hearing loss.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Cerumen (earwax) impaction / obstructive conductive hearing loss
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Doctor explicitly suspected impacted wax as an initial and common cause of unilateral muffled hearing; patient reports unilateral muffled hearing without pain/discharge and no other red flags. Symptoms intermittent and can be masked by external sound—compatible with conductive obstruction.
supporting_evidence: Unilateral muffled hearing (left) for six weeks
No ear pain, no discharge, no fever (makes acute infection less likely)
Doctor specifically suggested wax as likely and recommended otoscopic exam
Tinnitus can occur with conductive hearing loss and be masked by external sound
opposing_evidence: Tinnitus and mild imbalance can also indicate inner-ear (sensorineural) pathology which would not be resolved by wax removal
Patient's statement about using cotton buds (‘I'll do it’) may be ambiguous; if he routinely cleans ears, wax impaction is possible but not confirmed

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic triad of unilateral hearing loss, unilateral tinnitus, and imbalance/vestibular symptoms fits vestibular schwannoma. The subacute progressive unilateral nature over weeks raises this possibility and warrants otologic evaluation and audiometry/imaging if otoscopy is normal.
supporting_evidence: Unilateral (left) hearing loss and unilateral tinnitus
Mild imbalance/dizziness consistent with vestibular nerve involvement
opposing_evidence: No focal neurological signs reported and symptom severity is relatively mild
Vestibular schwannoma is less common than more benign causes (wax, middle ear disease)
No audiometry or imaging done yet to confirm sensorineural pattern

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral cochleitis / labyrinthitis or otitis media with inner-ear involvement
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Inflammation/infection of the inner or middle ear can produce unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus and dizziness; viral etiologies can be subacute and sometimes lack fever or significant otalgia. Should be considered after cerumen is excluded.
supporting_evidence: Unilateral hearing change with tinnitus and intermittent dizziness/nausea
Possible prior brief episode a year ago suggests episodic inflammatory events could recur
opposing_evidence: No ear pain, no discharge, no fever—less typical for bacterial otitis media or acute otitis externa
Dizziness is mild and not the severe vertigo classically seen with acute labyrinthitis

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Meniere disease causes episodic unilateral tinnitus, fluctuating hearing loss and episodic vertigo. Patient has unilateral tinnitus/hearing symptoms and intermittent imbalance, but the dizziness described is mild (not the severe rotational vertigo typical of Meniere) and there is no clear pattern of discrete vertigo attacks.
supporting_evidence: Unilateral tinnitus and fluctuating hearing symptoms
opposing_evidence: Dizziness is not described as severe spinning vertigo or discrete episodes lasting minutes-to-hours as typical for Meniere
No documented low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (no audiogram yet)
